theory.intro: The **expected value** $E(X)$ is the long-run average of $X$ over many repeats of an experiment. Multiply each value by its probability and add the results. It is also written $\mu$, the mean of the distribution.
facts: $E(X)=\mu=\sum xP(x)$: multiply each value by its probability, then add every product.
$E(X)$ is the average value of $X$ over many repeats, not the result of a single trial.
The expected value need not be a value $X$ can take: an expected $2.4$ children is a valid mean.
$E(X)$ and the most likely value are different concepts and need not coincide; the most likely value is the one with the greatest probability.
Check that the probabilities add to $1$ before finding $E(X)$.
A negative value of $x$ contributes a negative term $xP(x)$ to the sum.
steps: Check that the probabilities add to $1$.
Multiply each value $x$ by its probability $P(x)$.

workedExamples.solution_text:
Multiply each outcome by its probability.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc}x&-2&0&3&5\\\hline P(X=x)&0.2&0.1&0.4&0.3\\xP(X=x)&-0.4&0&1.2&1.5\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}E(X)&=-0.4+0+1.2+1.5\\&=2.3\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A distribution is given by $\left(0,\frac14\right)$, $\left(2,\frac12\right)$ and $\left(4,\frac14\right)$. Find $E(X)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Each pair gives an outcome and its probability.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&0&2&4\\[6pt]\hline P(X=x)&\frac14&\frac12&\frac14\\[6pt]xP(X=x)&0&1&1\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}E(X)&=0+1+1\\&=2\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A random variable has $P(x)=\frac{x+1}{12}$ for $x\in\{1,3,5\}$. Find $E(X)$ in exact form.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Substitute each outcome into the probability rule, then calculate the products.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&1&3&5\\[6pt]\hline P(x)&\frac{2}{12}&\frac{4}{12}&\frac{6}{12}\\[6pt]xP(x)&\frac{2}{12}&\frac{12}{12}&\frac{30}{12}\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}E(X)&=\frac{2+12+30}{12}\\&=\frac{44}{12}\\&=\frac{11}{3}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A random variable has $P(x)=k(x+2)$ for $x\in\{0,1,2\}$. Find $k$ and $E(X)$.

A bag contains four white marbles and two black marbles. Two marbles are selected at random without replacement. Let $X$ be the number of black marbles selected. Construct the probability distribution and find $E(X)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
For exactly one black marble, include both drawing orders.
$\begin{align*}P(X=0)&=\frac46\times\frac35\\&=\frac25\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}P(X=1)&=\frac26\times\frac45+\frac46\times\frac25\\&=\frac{8}{15}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}P(X=2)&=\frac26\times\frac15\\&=\frac{1}{15}\end{align*}$
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&0&1&2\\[6pt]\hline P(X=x)&\frac25&\frac{8}{15}&\frac{1}{15}\\[6pt]xP(X=x)&0&\frac{8}{15}&\frac{2}{15}\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}E(X)&=0+\frac{8}{15}+\frac{2}{15}\\&=\frac23\end{align*}$
Over many repeats, the average number of black marbles selected is $\frac23$ per pair.

workedExamples.question_text:
The distribution below has $E(X)=3.4$. Find $p$ and $q$ by setting up two equations.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&1&3&5\\\hline P(X=x)&p&0.4&q\end{array}$
workedExamples.solution_text:
Use the probability total and the expected value.
$\begin{align*}p+0.4+q&=1\\p+q&=0.6\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}1p+3(0.4)+5q&=3.4\\p+5q&=2.2\end{align*}$
Substitute $p=0.6-q$ into the second equation.
$\begin{align*}0.6-q+5q&=2.2\\4q&=1.6\\q&=0.4\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}p&=0.6-0.4\\&=0.2\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Two players have expected numbers of goals per match of $1.7$ and $1.5$. Who scores more goals per match in the long run? Explain why an expected value of $1.7$ is sensible even though goals are counted in whole numbers. Find each player's expected total over $20$ matches and explain whether these totals are guaranteed.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The first player has the greater expected value, so their average number of goals per match is higher over many matches.
An expected value of $1.7$ describes a long-run average. It need not be a possible score in one match.
For the first player, the expected total over $20$ matches is $20(1.7)=34$ goals.
For the second player, the expected total over $20$ matches is $20(1.5)=30$ goals.
These are expected totals, not guaranteed results.

foundation.question_text:
The table shows the distribution of $X$, the number of tries a player scores in a match.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.15 & 0.25 & 0.45 & 0.15 \end{array}$
Find $E(X)$.

Find the expected value of the random variable $X$.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1 \end{array}$

A distribution is given by the ordered pairs $\left(0,\frac{1}{8}\right)$, $\left(1,\frac{3}{8}\right)$, $\left(2,\frac{3}{8}\right)$, $\left(3,\frac{1}{8}\right)$.
Find $E(X)$.

A random variable has $P(x)=\frac{x}{15}$ for $x \in \{1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5\}$.
Find $E(X)$ in exact form.

A survey finds that $X$, the number of bicycles owned by a household, has $E(X)=2.4$.
Explain what this means, and why $2.4$ is a sensible answer even though no household owns $2.4$ bicycles.
foundation.solution_text:
Over a large number of households, the average number of bicycles per household is $2.4$.
The expected value is a long-run average, so it does not have to be one of the values $X$ can take.

foundation.question_text:

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & -3 & -1 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.25 & 0.15 \end{array}$
Find $E(X)$.

development.question_text:
The distribution of $X$ is given below.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.15 & k & 0.35 & 0.2 \end{array}$
Find $k$ and hence $E(X)$.

The relative frequencies below estimate the distribution of $X$, the number of children in a randomly chosen family.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.42 & 0.22 & 0.21 & 0.1 & 0.05 \end{array}$
Find the expected number of children per family.

A box holds six tiles: two marked $1$, three marked $4$ and one marked $10$.
One tile is drawn at random and $X$ is the number on it.
Build the probability distribution and find $E(X)$.
development.solution_text:
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 4 & 10 \\ \hline P(X=x) & \frac{2}{6} & \frac{3}{6} & \frac{1}{6} \end{array}$
$\frac{2}{6}+\frac{3}{6}+\frac{1}{6}=1$, so the distribution is complete.
$E(X)=1\left(\frac{2}{6}\right)+4\left(\frac{3}{6}\right)+10\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)$
$=\frac{2+12+10}{6}$
$=\frac{24}{6}$
$=4$

development.question_text:
A random variable has $P(x)=\frac{x+2}{28}$ for $x \in \{2,\ 4,\ 6,\ 8\}$.
Find $E(X)$ in exact form.

The random variable $X$ has $E(X)=3.5$.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.2 & p & 0.3 & q \end{array}$
Find $p$ and $q$ by setting up two equations.

Two goalkeepers' saving records give the distributions below for the number of penalties saved per match.
$\text{Amina: } \begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.2 \end{array}$
$\text{Bea: } \begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.15 & 0.25 & 0.25 & 0.35 \end{array}$
Who saves more penalties per match in the long run?
development.solution_text:
$E(\text{Amina})=0(0.1)+1(0.3)+2(0.4)+3(0.2)$
$=1.7$
$E(\text{Bea})=0(0.15)+1(0.25)+2(0.25)+3(0.35)$
$=1.8$
Bea has the greater expected value, so over many matches she saves more penalties per match.

mastery.question_text:
The distribution $(1,a)$, $\left(2,0.15\right)$, $(3,b)$, $\left(4,0.3\right)$, $\left(5,0.25\right)$ has mean $3.45$.
Find $a$ and $b$.

A random variable has $P(x)=k(x+1)$ for $x \in \{1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5\}$.
Find $k$ and $E(X)$.

A hen lays $0$, $1$ or $2$ eggs on a day with probabilities $0.2$, $0.5$ and $0.3$.
How many eggs should the farmer expect from this hen over a $7$-day week, and why is that figure not guaranteed?
mastery.solution_text:
$E(X)=0(0.2)+1(0.5)+2(0.3)$
$=0+0.5+0.6$
$=1.1$
Expected eggs in $7$ days $=7(1.1)$
$=7.7$
The expected value is a long-run average per day, so an individual week can give any whole number of eggs from $0$ to $14$.
